legacy_report:
SOURCE: Deep Networks with Stochastic Depth. Gao Huang, Yu Sun, Zhuang Liu, Daniel Sedra, Kilian Q. Weinberger (Cornell and Tsinghua). ECCV 2016. The file is arXiv:1603.09382v3, dated 28 Jul 2016.

COVERAGE: I read all 42,848 of 42,848 chars, which is pages 1–16. That covers the body, both tables, Figs 1–8 and the references. The paper has no appendix. I did not run figures.py, because the captions came through in the text extraction.

CLAIMS
- claim: The method drops whole ResBlocks at random for each mini-batch during training. The survival probability falls linearly from 1 at the input to p_L=0.5 at the last block. At test time every block is active and its output is multiplied by p_l.
  number: p_L = 0.5; E(L~) ≈ 3L/4
  setup: Applies to all experiments. For the 110-layer ResNet with L=54 blocks, the expected depth is about 40 blocks.
  quote: "p𝓁 = 1− 𝓁/L(1− pL)" … "E(˜L) = (3L− 1)/4, or E(˜L)≈ 3L/4" … "H Test𝓁 = ReLU(p𝓁f𝓁(H Test𝓁−1 ; W𝓁) + H Test𝓁−1 )"
  where: pp. 5–7
- claim: Stochastic depth lowers test error against the same ResNet trained at constant depth, using identical optimisation settings.
  number: CIFAR-10+ 6.41→5.25; CIFAR-100+ 27.76→24.98; SVHN 1.80→1.75
  setup: 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR with flip and translate augmentation, SGD for 500 epochs, batch 128. SVHN uses a 152-layer ResNet for 50 epochs with no augmentation. Each reported error is from the epoch with the lowest validation error.
  quote: "ResNet with constant depth 6.41 27.76 1.80 21.78 / ResNet with stochastic depth 5.25 24.98 1.75 21.98"; "relative improvement of 18%"
  where: Table 1, p. 7; p. 8
  The gain also holds without augmentation: "13.63% and 44.74% … resulting in test errors of 11.66% and 37.8%" (p. 9).
- claim: Training wall-clock time drops by about 25%, which matches the expected-depth calculation. Setting p_L lower saves more time.
  number: 25%; 40% at p_L=0.2
  setup: Same runs as Table 1. At p_L=0.2 the 110-layer CIFAR-10 model ties the baseline.
  quote: "Constant Depth 20h 42m 20h 51m 33h 43m / Stochastic Depth 15h 7m 15h 20m 25h 33m"; "Stochastic depth consistently gives a 25% speedup"; "with pL = 0.2 … same test error as its constant depth counterpart on CIFAR-10 but gives a 40% speedup"
  where: Table 2, p. 10; p. 6
- claim: With stochastic depth, a 1202-layer ResNet beats the 110-layer one. Trained at constant depth, the 1202-layer net does worse than the 110-layer net.
  number: 6.67% (constant) vs 4.91% (stochastic), a 27% relative gain
  setup: CIFAR-10+, 300 epochs, warm-up at LR 0.01 for 10 epochs, then 0.1, divided by 10 at epochs 150 and 225. This result is not included in Table 1.
  quote: "training with stochastic depth leads to a 27% relative improvement" … "from 110 layers to 1202 yields a further improvement on the previous record-low 5.25%, to a 4.91% test error without sign of overfitting"
  where: pp. 10–11
- claim: The linear decay rule beats the uniform rule at every p_L tested, and it holds up when p_L is anywhere from 0.4 to 0.8. A network needs enough depth before the method helps.
  number: p_L 0.4–0.8
  setup: 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-10, with p_L swept from 0.1 to 1.0 (Fig. 8). A heatmap crosses p_L with depths of 20–110 layers.
  quote: "the linear decay rule outperforms the uniform rule consistently; 3) the linear decay rule is relatively robust to fluctuations in pL and obtains competitive results when pL ranges from 0.4 to 0.8"
  where: p. 13
- claim: Against Dropout, the authors report that Dropout barely helps a ResNet that uses BatchNorm, while stochastic depth still regularises.
  number: none
  setup: 110-layer ResNet with BN on CIFAR-10. The Dropout rates are not reported.
  quote: "Dropout gives practically no improvement when used on 110-layer ResNets with Batch Normalization"
  where: p. 4

LIMITS
- ImageNet shows no gain. With a 152-layer ResNet, error at 90 epochs is 23.38% against the baseline's 23.06%. At 120 epochs it is 21.98% against 21.78%. The authors concede "no immediate benefit … on this particular architecture" (pp. 11–12).
- Every result is a single run, with no seeds or error bars.
- The SVHN gain is small: 1.80 vs 1.75.
- The authors note "slightly higher fluctuations" in test error (p. 9).
- The vanishing-gradient evidence is one plot: gradient magnitude at the first conv layer (Fig. 7).
- Ensemble interpretation: the paper offers it as an explanation and never tests it.
- Shallow networks: they need less aggressive skipping.
- Dated: state-of-the-art claims are as of March 2016, and the authors footnote that later work has improved on them.

BUILDS ON: He et al., ResNet (arXiv 2015) [8], with Identity Mappings (2016) [35]. Srivastava et al., Dropout (JMLR 2014) [16]. Ioffe and Szegedy, Batch Normalization (2015) [14]. Srivastava, Greff and Schmidhuber, Highway Networks (2015) [15, 29]. DropConnect, Wan et al. (ICML 2013) [20]. DropIn, Smith et al. (CVPR 2016) [22]. Bengio et al. on vanishing gradients (1994) [11]. The code base is fb.resnet.torch, Gross and Wilber (2016) [34].

CODE: The paper prints no code. It gives a Torch 7 repository: github.com/yueatsprograms/Stochastic_Depth (p. 8).

FIGURES: Fig. 2, p. 5: "The linear decay of p𝓁 illustrated on a ResNet with stochastic depth for p0 =1 and pL = 0.5." It shows on one diagram that whole blocks are skipped and how p_l falls with depth. Second choice: Fig. 8 (left), p. 13, which compares linear and uniform rules against the constant-depth baseline across p_L and is the ablation in one plot.

PROBLEMS: The CIFAR-100 constant-depth baseline is reported three ways. Table 1 gives 27.76, the text on p. 9 says "test error of 27.22%", and the Fig. 3 label reads 27.88%. Please cite the Table 1 value, or flag the mismatch. The Fig. 8 data labels came out as a jumbled list of numbers, so I could not tie them to points and have not quoted them. The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
